'''Catharine Anastasia Conley''' (born October 9, 1966<ref name="McGehee"/>) is an American scientist known for her research on [[plants in space]]. She was [[NASA]]'s 6th Planetary Protection Officer from 2006 through 2018.

==Early life==
Catharine Anastasia Conley was born on October 9, 1966 to mathematician [[Charles Cameron Conley]] and geneticist Catharine "Kit" Smith.<ref name="McGehee">McGehee, Richard (1988). [https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~mcgehee/publications/McGehee1988/McGehee1988ErgodThDynamSys8p1.pdf Charles C. Conley, 1933–1984]. ''Ergod. Th. & Dynam. Sys.'' (1988), 8*, 1-7.</ref>

==Education==
Conley received her bachelor's from [[MIT]], a Ph.D. in Plant Biology from [[Cornell University]] in 1994,<ref name="thesis-conley-1995">{{cite thesis |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/304187201/ |title=Spatial and temporal localization of the defects associated with Petunia cytoplasmic male sterility |date=1995 |publisher=[[Cornell University]] |type=Ph.D. |last=Conley |first=Catharine Anastasia |id={{ProQuest|304187201}} |url-access=subscription  |oclc=693242966}}</ref> and obtained a postdoctoral fellow position at The [[Scripps Research Institute]] studying proteins involved in muscle contraction.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.biomedexperts.com/Profile.bme/259083/Catharine_A_Conley |title=Catharine Conley |access-date=May 4, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716214649/http://www.biomedexperts.com/Profile.bme/259083/Catharine_A_Conley |archive-date=July 16, 2011 |url-status=dead |df=mdy-all }}</ref><ref>{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20130416091605/http://www.wormbase.org/db/misc/person?name=WBPerson116;class=Person|title=Person Report: Catharine Conley}}</ref> Conley conducted some of her research using the nematode ''[[Caenorhabditis elegans]]''.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20071130154023/http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/science/experiments/ICE-First.html International Caenorhabditis elegans Experiment: Physiological Study of Nematode Worms in Weightlessness (ICE-First)] 2009-02-20</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.descsite.nl/NL-taxi/ICE/ICE-page1.htm |title=International Ceonorhabditis elegans Experiment First flight: Science Goals and Objectives |work=Dutch Experimental Support Center |first=Michel |last=Viso}}</ref>

==NASA career==
In 1999 Conley became a research scientist with the NASA [[Ames Research Center]]. Her research focuses on the evolution of motility, particularly animal muscle. One of her experiments was on board during the [[Space Shuttle Columbia disaster]]. The experiment, the fourteenth Biological Research In Canisters (BRIC-14), survived re-entry and the nematode cultures were still alive. Some scientific data was recovered.<ref>[http://www.astrobio.net/news/article1821.html Columbia Survivors] 2006-01-01 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070125150703/http://www.astrobio.net/news/article1821.html |date=January 25, 2007 }}</ref>

In 2006, Conley was appointed as NASA's Planetary Protection Officer (see [[Planetary protection]]), replacing John Rummel.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/10/09/science/09clea.html?pagewanted=all |title=In NASA's Sterile Areas, Plenty of Robust Bacteria |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=October 9, 2007 |first=Warren E. |last=Leary}}</ref><ref>[http://www.astrobio.net/news/article2514.html Shades of Gravity: Interview with Catharine Conley] 2007-11-05{{dead link|date=April 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.lpi.usra.edu/meetings/msr2008/pdf/4060.pdf |title=Planetary protection considerations for Mars sample return |date=March 2008 |first=Catharine A. |last=Conley |work=[[Lunar and Planetary Institute]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://quest.arc.nasa.gov/people/bios/astrobiology/conley.html |title=Meet Cassie Conley |access-date=May 4, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090420042818/http://quest.arc.nasa.gov/people/bios/astrobiology/conley.html |archive-date=April 20, 2009 |url-status=dead |df=mdy-all }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090510124813/http://quest.nasa.gov/projects/spacewardbound/atacama2006/bios/Cassie_Conley.html |archive-date=May 10, 2009 |url-status=dead |df=mdy-all }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://pipl.com/directory/people/Catharine/Conley |title=Catharine Conley Pipl Profile |access-date=May 4, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111002001432/http://pipl.com/directory/people/Catharine/Conley |archive-date=October 2, 2011 |url-status=dead |df=mdy-all }}</ref> A NASA re-organization opened the job for competition in 2017, and Conley was replaced by Dr. [[Lisa Pratt]] in February 2018.<ref name="sj-2018feb22">{{cite journal |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/nasa-planetary-protection-officer-suggests-loosening-limits-exploring-mars-life |title=NASA planetary protection officer suggests loosening limits on |url=https://news.iu.edu/stories/2018/01/iub/releases/18-lisa-pratt-planetary-protection-officer.html |title=Indiana University astrobiologist named planetary protection officer at NASA |date=January 18, 2018 |publisher=[[Indiana University]]}}</ref>

During her time at NASA, Conley worked with protecting life on [[Mars]], focusing on keeping Earth's bacteria off Mars when doing research. This aligns with The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, which aims to keep contamination from Earth to other planets in check. Conley's biggest concern of contamination was transferring lichen from Earth to Mars. Both planets have similar requirements which allows lichen to grow. To address these concerns, NASA used the [[Curiosity (rover)|Curisosity]] rover, which surveys Mars' environment to see if it can support microbial life.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2015-10-05 |title=Mars Is Pretty Clean. Her Job at NASA Is to Keep It That Way. (Published 2015) |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/10/06/science/mars-catharine-conley-nasa-planetary-protection-officer.html |access-date=2025-11-06 |language=en}}</ref> The rover itself could contaminate Mars with microbes from Earth. To combat this issue, the landers used in missions are sterilized in an oven and kept in a bioshield until they reach Mars.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Biba |first=Erin |date=2014-10-01 |title=Meet NASA's One and Only Planetary Protection Officer |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/meet-nasa-s-one-and-only-planetary-protection-officer/ |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=Scientific American |language=en}}</ref>
